blogs.title: Standing Strikes Again: D.C. Circuit Tosses AFL’s OSC-FOIA Challenge for Lack of Injury
blogs.description: This post analyzes the D.C. Circuit’s threshold ruling that America First Legal lacked Article III standing to compel the Office of Special Counsel to investigate DOJ’s alleged FOIA practices. It unpacks the court’s injury, causation, and redressability analysis; the rejection of both asserted informational injuries; and the opinion’s reliance on Summers, Akins, Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, and Haaland to tighten the chain between the plaintiff’s harms and an order binding OSC.

blogs.title: When ‘Shall Investigate’ Isn’t a Right to Know: Informational Standing After Akins
blogs.description: Focusing on the opinion’s treatment of informational injury, this piece explains why a statutory duty to investigate under 5 U.S.C. § 1216(a)(3) does not create a cognizable right to receive information, distinguishing FOIA and FACA-style disclosure regimes. It explores the court’s view that § 1216 lacks a disclosure entitlement and that § 1214’s notice provisions are discretionary in § 1216 investigations (citing Carson), and considers the implications for watchdog groups seeking to leverage ‘shall investigate’ clauses for standing.

blogs.title: The FOIA–OSC Interface Left Unresolved: Does § 1216 Impose a Non-Discretionary Duty?
blogs.description: The district court concluded OSC misread FOIA’s § 552(a)(4)(F) and that § 1216 independently authorizes OSC to investigate alleged arbitrary FOIA withholdings, but the D.C. Circuit vacated on standing without reaching that merits question. This post canvasses the statutory architecture—§ 1216(a)(3), § 1216(c), § 1214, § 1215, and FOIA § 552(a)(4)(F)—and outlines the competing readings of whether § 1216’s ‘shall conduct an investigation’ is judicially enforceable, what decisions are committed to agency discretion, and what questions remain open in the D.C. Circuit after the vacatur.

blogs.title: Redressability and Independent Actors: AHM’s Shadow Over Administrative Challenges
blogs.description: The panel’s redressability analysis leans on the Supreme Court’s admonition against speculation about ‘unfettered choices’ by actors not before the court. This post examines how Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine and Haaland frame redressability around binding relief on the parties, why the court rejected causal chains running through OSC’s enforcement discretion, the MSPB, and DOJ, and how that approach constrains suits that try to influence one agency by ordering another to act.

blogs.title: Heckler by Another Name: Using Standing to Police Separation of Powers in Enforcement
blogs.description: Linking the opinion to Heckler v. Chaney, this post argues that the D.C. Circuit used standing’s causation and redressability prongs to avoid entangling courts in executive enforcement choices. It discusses the doctrinal tension between a statute’s mandatory-sounding ‘shall investigate’ and the judiciary’s reluctance to compel investigations or predict enforcement outcomes, and assesses the opinion as part of a broader trend channeling challenges to executive nonenforcement out of federal court.

blogs.title: FOIA Discipline Reality Check: Why § 552(a)(4)(F) Remains the True Gatekeeper
blogs.description: For FOIA litigants aiming to trigger OSC discipline, this case underscores the practical necessity of meeting § 552(a)(4)(F)’s predicates—a court order compelling disclosure, a fee award, and a finding questioning arbitrariness or caprice. The post outlines why attempts to bypass that pathway via § 1216 face standing obstacles, and offers tactical takeaways for FOIA plaintiffs seeking language in judicial orders that will obligate OSC to initiate disciplinary proceedings.

blogs.title: Organizational Litigation After Hecate: The Perils of Speculative Causal Chains
blogs.description: This post distills lessons for advocacy groups pressing structural or policy claims through multi-agency causal theories. Drawing on Hecate Energy and this decision, it highlights pleading pitfalls when relief depends on a string of discretionary choices by independent actors, offers strategies to ground redressability in orders that bind the defendant agency, and cautions against piggybacking ‘informational injury’ on separate ongoing FOIA suits.

blogs.title: Vacatur and the Vanishing Merits: Jurisdictional Clean-Up in AFL v. Greer
blogs.description: The court vacated the district court’s merits ruling and ordered dismissal for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. This post explains the consequences of jurisdictional vacatur for preclusion and persuasive authority, how it erases the district court’s statutory interpretation of § 1216 versus § 552(a)(4)(F), and what that means for future litigants seeking to press the same statutory arguments in a better vehicle.
